Reel

extensions prototype

Both extensions on simulated glass. The phone below is inside some other app — a job form, a recruiter thread — and Reel rides over it: the dial on Android, the keyboard on iOS. The vault comes preloaded as Alex Rivera, a demo applicant; anything you add stays in this browser only. A webpage can't reach into real apps, so judge the speed and the feel here, not the reach.

Test 1 · the dial · Android

Apply to Northbeam using only the dial

The phone is inside Northbeam's careers app. The round button on its edge is Reel — it floats over whatever app you're in. Fill the whole application without ever leaving the form.

No overlays on iOS — the dial is Android's. On iPad the vault rides the keyboard, the share sheet, and the Files app instead.

The moves

Tap the round buttonOpens and stays. Copied something just before? The dial catches it — or offers to, depending on the catch switch below. Spin the ring: it steps one item at a time and settles — a fast flick carries a few extra clicks; the item at the index mark is up. Tap it — copied, receipt, and the box you were in grows a Paste chip: tap that and the job is done. Tap the glass centre to put the dial away.
One ring, everything on itYour two pinned items hold the edge slots — same place forever, tap to use — and everything else follows, newest first, all types together. Colour says the type: amber is text, rust is a link, violet is an image.
Hold · slide out · releaseOne finger, never lifting. Hold the button and slide out onto the ring, then arc your finger to spin it. Release on an item to take it and put the dial away.
Hold · dragDrag the button anywhere and let go — it clings to the nearest frame edge, at the height you left it, and stays there.
Double-tap the buttonYour most recent item, instantly. No dial.
Hold — it comes to youHold, and the ring comes to you. Hold an off-center item and the ring walks it to the index mark, then stops. Hold either end of the arc — or drag past it and stay — and the ring keeps cruising from that end, gathering speed, until you let go.

The switches below — Catch style, Egress, Preview and Peek — change how it feels. Flip one, run the errand again. Copy something in another app pretends you copied elsewhere; Replay first run shows the one-time permission moment.

Preview: what's up shows at the top of the phone's screen, so your eyes can stay up there while your thumb spins down here.

Style tries five ways the ring can mark what it holds — today's chips down to bare dots. Same metal, same moves; rule by eye.

Peek answers "what's coming": Neighbors sits the previous and next item beside the floating preview — tap one to step; Fan flashes every visible label outward the moment the dial opens. Rule by feel.

＋ Make it yours

Add your own resume or a photo — a photo joins the dial, a document shows up when you attach inside the form. The file never uploads; only its name is remembered, in your browser.

Also: select any text on this page and a Save to Reel chip appears — write one line of your own cover letter, select it, save it, reuse it on the keyboard page.

Test 2 · the keyboard · iOS

Second application of the day — this time on the iPhone

This is the iOS surface: your stuff rides the keyboard. Tap into any box on the phone and the vault comes up first — you drop in, take what you came for, and leave. On Android the dial carries this job instead.

This keyboard is iPhone and iPad. The frame you picked is Android hardware — there, the dial is how the vault travels.

Three things to try

Tap a box, tap a tileThe vault opens first — pins up front, newest after, everything in one strip. A tile lands right at your cursor, done. A box that can't take a thing just dims it: tap into Email and watch the images grey out; the message box lights everything back up.
Tap the password boxiOS hands passwords to Apple's own keyboard, automatically. Watch the swap — nothing custom ever sees a password.
LeaveOne tap on back to your keyboard and you're typing on your own again. iOS brings up whichever keyboard you used last, so a fast exit is part of the design.

Also here: search runs on our own keys (a keyboard can't summon a keyboard), and the Interview thanks tile asks you to fill a blank before it inserts. Replay first run below shows the one-time Full Access moment — try both answers.

A photo you add joins the strip; a document shows up when you attach inside the form. Nothing uploads — only the name is remembered.
